questions.q: tasks.js has const tasks = []; and let nextId = 3; (not exported), and exports addTask(title). Why is this a good design?
questions.explain: Without an export, no other file can reach tasks or nextId. All changes go through addTask, which keeps the ids correct.
options: Other files can reset nextId when they need to
The only way to add a task is through addTask, so ids can never be duplicated
Unexported variables are faster to read

questions.q: In an ES module, which import of tasks.js from the same folder is correct?
questions.explain: A relative import starts with ./ (this folder) or ../ (the folder above) and includes the file extension. Without ./, Node.js looks for a package in node_modules.

questions.q: You run node main.js and see SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module. What is the usual fix?
questions.explain: Without "type": "module", Node.js treats .js files as CommonJS, where import is not allowed.
options: Add "type": "module" to package.json, for example with npm pkg set type=module
Move the import lines to the bottom of the file

questions.q: This file exports addTask and keeps tasks private. What does it print?
questions.explain: export does not change how the code inside the file works. Two tasks are added, so the second gets id 3 and there are 3 tasks. Only other files are kept away from tasks.

questions.q:
task-store.js has export default class TaskStore { … }. Another file writes:

import Store from "./task-store.js";
import Whatever from "./task-store.js";

What happens?
questions.explain: The importer picks any name for a default export: import Store from "./task-store.js" and import Whatever from "./task-store.js" give the same class under two names.
options: Only Store works, because it is imported first
Both throw, because the class is called TaskStore
They are two different copies of the class

questions.q: Why does the lesson say to prefer named exports?
questions.explain: With a default export, every file can call the same thing something different, and a misspelled default import is just a new name. A typo in a named import is an error. ZudoJS only uses named exports.
options: Default exports are slower to load
They keep one name for one thing, so search and rename work, and a typo is an error
Named exports are the only kind CommonJS understands

questions.q: tasks.js and users.js both export a function called create. How do you use both in main.js?
questions.explain: as renames an import in the current file. Inside main.js, the two functions are now createTask and createUser.
options: You cannot: one module must rename its function
import { create as createTask } from "./tasks.js"; and import { create as createUser } from "./users.js";

questions.q: What does import * as taskModule from "./tasks.js"; give you?
questions.explain: This is a namespace import. You then write taskModule.count(items), which makes it obvious where count comes from. Unexported names are still hidden.
options: A copy of the file's source code
One object that holds every export of tasks.js as a property
Every variable in tasks.js, exported or not

questions.q: Renaming with as in an import works like renaming in destructuring. What does this print?
questions.explain: The two create functions live on under new names, createTask and createUser. No variable called create exists in this file.

questions.q: counter.js prints counter.js is running at the top. Both tasks.js and users.js import it, and main.js imports both. How many times is the message printed?
questions.explain: However many files import a module, its code runs once. Every importer gets the same exports.
options: Once: a module runs only the first time it is imported
Never, because imported files do not run

questions.q: To give each part its own counter, counter.js can export a function that creates one. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call to makeCounter creates a new count, so the task and user counters are separate. Compare with a shared module-level count, which would give task-1 user-2 task-3.

questions.q: Your project has "type": "module". How do you make one file CommonJS?
questions.explain: In a "type": "module" project, .js files are ES modules and .cjs files are CommonJS. Without "type": "module", every .js file is CommonJS.
options: You cannot mix them in one project

questions.q: Which statement about require is true?
questions.explain: require is a normal function call that loads synchronously. import is special syntax. For new code, always write ES modules.
options: It is special syntax that Node.js reads before running anything
It is an ordinary function that loads the file right then and returns its module.exports
It works in the browser terminal too
It is the recommended way to load modules in new code

questions.q: const { addTask } = require("./tasks.cjs") is just destructuring the object that require returns. This file imitates that with a plain object. What does it print?
questions.explain: Destructuring picks functions out of the object; renaming them does not change the object's keys. Both functions share the same tasks array.

questions.q: This file is an ES module. What does it print?
questions.explain: require and module only exist in CommonJS files. In an ES module they do not exist, and typeof on an unknown name gives "undefined" instead of throwing.
questions.code:
export const LIMIT = 20;
console.log(typeof require, typeof module, LIMIT);

questions.q: An ES module writes import tasks from "./tasks.cjs";. What is tasks?
questions.explain: An ES module can import CommonJS: its module.exports arrives as the default export, and Node.js also detects simple named exports. The reverse, require in an ES module, does not exist.
options: An error: ES modules cannot import CommonJS files
The CommonJS file's module.exports object, arriving as the default export
Only the first function in the file

questions.q: A tasks/ folder has store.js (exports insert, all), service.js (exports createTask, listTasks) and index.js with export { createTask, listTasks } from "./service.js";. What does the rest of the app see through index.js?
questions.explain: export { … } from re-exports without importing into index.js. The entry point is the feature's public face: insert stays internal.
options: Nothing, because index.js does not import anything

questions.q: Why should the rest of the app not import insert straight from tasks/store.js?
questions.explain: Going through the entry point means every task is validated, and you can later replace store.js with a real database without changing any other file. That line is a module boundary.
options: It would let code store a task that skipped the validation in createTask, and tie other files to an internal detail
Because relative imports only work one folder deep

questions.q: Why do you write import { NotFoundError } from "@zudojs/errors" and not a path to a file deep inside the package?
questions.explain: npm packages draw the same public/internal line with "exports". Only the listed entry points can be imported.
options: Deep paths are slower to load
The package's "exports" field in package.json lists which paths may be imported; internals are not listed
npm deletes the files inside packages after installing them
Only the first file of a package can export anything

questions.q: This is the lesson's service.js and store.js put in one file. What does it print?
questions.explain: createTask trims and rejects the empty title. all() returns copies, so changing the copy does not change the stored row.
options:
title must not be empty
[ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false } ]

title must not be empty
[ { id: 1, title: 'HACKED', done: false } ]
[ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false }, { id: 2, title: '', done: false } ]

title must not be empty
[ { id: 1, title: '  Buy milk ', done: false } ]

questions.q: tasks.js imports logger.js, and logger.js imports DEFAULT_PRIORITY from tasks.js and uses it at its top level. main.js imports tasks.js. What happens with ES modules?
questions.explain: Node.js runs logger.js first, because tasks.js needs it. logger.js reads DEFAULT_PRIORITY before the line in tasks.js that creates it has run: the temporal dead zone, across two files.
options: It works, and prints the default priority
The value is quietly undefined, with a warning

questions.q: In the circular import, logger.js reads DEFAULT_PRIORITY before tasks.js has run its const line. This one-file version has the same order problem. What does it print?
questions.explain: A const used before its line has run is in the temporal dead zone and throws a ReferenceError. In the circular import, "before its line has run" happens across two files.

questions.q: What happens with the same circular dependency written in CommonJS with require?
questions.explain: CommonJS is worse: the program keeps running with undefined and prints "default priority undefined". A loud crash is easier to find than a silent wrong value.
options: It crashes with the same ReferenceError
Nothing crashes: require returns the half-finished exports, the value is quietly undefined, and you get only a warning
Node.js refuses to start and asks you to rename the files
It works perfectly, because CommonJS supports cycles

questions.q: What is the fix the lesson shows for the tasks.js ↔ logger.js cycle?
questions.explain: With constants.js, dependencies point one way only: tasks.js → logger.js → constants.js and tasks.js → constants.js. Passing the value as an argument, or merging the modules, also works.
options: Move DEFAULT_PRIORITY into a third module, constants.js, that imports neither of them

questions.q: users.js and tasks.js import each other, but each uses the imported function only inside its own functions, never at the top level. What is true?
questions.explain: By the time a function is called, both modules have finished loading. Only top-level use hits the error. Still, move the shared logic into a third module or pass the function in as an argument.
options: It usually does not crash, but it is still a warning sign: the modules cannot be understood or tested separately
It is the recommended way to share code between features

questions.q: Which rule for a feature-based layout prevents most circular dependencies?
questions.explain: If shared/ never imports from features, arrows only point from features to shared code, never back. Features import each other only through their index.js.
options: Every feature imports every other feature's store.js
Shared code lives in shared/ and never imports from a feature
Each feature has exactly one file

questions.q: The practice compares due dates written as YYYY-MM-DD text. What does this print?
questions.explain: Dates in YYYY-MM-DD form sort correctly as text, so < works. A task that is done is never overdue.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Page 3 is items 41 to 60, and only 41 to 45 exist. Page 4 starts past the end, so slice gives an empty array.

questions.q: Finish the two named exports. formatTask(task) returns [x] title or [ ] title. isOverdue(task, today) is true when the task is not done and task.due < today. The program should print [ ] File taxes (overdue).
questions.explain: In a real project these would live in format.js and dates.js, and main.js would import them by name. YYYY-MM-DD strings compare correctly with <.

questions.q: This CommonJS module is being rewritten as an ES module with named exports. Finish paginate(items, page): page 1 is the first LIMIT items, page 2 the next, and so on. The program should print 20 [ 41, 42, 43, 44, 45 ].
questions.explain: export const and export function replace module.exports = { … }. Page n starts at index (n - 1) * LIMIT.

questions.q: Write the module's two exports. Keep tasks and nextId private (not exported). addTask(title) adds { id, title, done: false } with ids 1, 2, 3…; listTasks() returns copies of the tasks. The program should print [ 1, 2 ] Buy milk.
questions.explain: Only the two functions are exported. listTasks returns copies, so a caller changing a task cannot change the module's private data.

questions.q: A shared module-level counter gave task-1 user-2 task-3. Export makeCounter() instead, which returns a new, separate counter function each time. The program should print task-1 user-1 task-2.
questions.explain: A module runs once, so its top-level state is shared by every importer. A factory function gives each caller its own count through a closure.

questions.q: Finish the exported createTask(title). Trim the title; if it is empty, throw new Error("title must not be empty"); otherwise store it with the internal insert as { id, title, done: false }, where id is the number of stored tasks plus 1. The program should print title must not be empty and then [ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false } ].
questions.explain: insert is not exported, so the only way to store a task is createTask, which validates first. That is the idea of a module boundary.
questions.expected:
title must not be empty
[ { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false } ]

questions.q: An entry point should expose only the public functions. Build tasks as a frozen object with only createTask and listTasks (not insert), like import * as tasks would give from an index.js that re-exports those two. The program should print [ 'createTask', 'listTasks' ] 1.
questions.explain: The public face holds exactly two functions. insert exists, but the rest of the app cannot reach it, so every task goes through createTask.

questions.q: One way to break a cycle is to pass a value in as an argument instead of importing it. Finish makeLogger(defaultPriority): it returns a logChange(event, task) function that prints [tasks, default priority N] event: title. The program should print [tasks, default priority 3] created: Buy milk.
questions.explain: The logger no longer imports anything from the tasks module: it receives the value it needs. Dependencies then point one way only.

questions.q: Finish the named-export class TaskStore: add(title) throws new Error("store is full") when it already holds MAX_TASKS titles, otherwise it stores the title and returns the new count. The program should print 1 of 2, 2 of 2, store is full.
questions.explain: The lesson's version used export default class. As a named export, every file must import it as { TaskStore }, so the name stays the same everywhere.

questions.q: Write allowed(from, to), which checks two layout rules for an import from file from to file to (paths like src/tasks/service.js). Rule 1: a file in src/shared/ may not import from a feature (anything outside src/shared/). Rule 2: a file in one feature may import another feature only through its index.js. Everything else is allowed. The program should print true false true false.
questions.explain: Shared code never imports from a feature, which prevents most cycles. Features reach each other only through the public index.js, never into internals like store.js.

questions.q: tasks.js and users.js both import next from counter.js. A module runs once, so they share one count. This file puts the three together. What does it print?
questions.explain: There is only one count, so every call to next, from either side, moves it on. That is what sharing a module's state means.

questions.q: import * as taskModule from "./tasks.js" gives an object with every export as a property. This file builds a similar object by hand. What does it print?
questions.explain: Every export is a property of the namespace object, so taskModule.count makes it obvious where count comes from. Two of the three items are tasks.

questions.q: In a CommonJS cycle, require returns the half-finished exports object of the module that is still loading. This file imitates that. What does it print?
questions.explain: Reading a missing property gives undefined without an error. That is why a CommonJS cycle does not crash: it quietly uses the wrong value.
options: [tasks, default priority undefined] created: Buy milk
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: After the fix, constants.js runs first, then logger.js, then tasks.js. This file puts them together in that order. What does it print?
questions.explain: When dependencies point one way only, each module runs after the ones it needs, so every value exists before it is read.
options: [tasks, default priority undefined] created: Buy milk
